analysis.one_liner: Creates a public, searchable database of corporate crimes and enforcement actions.
analysis.headline: The bill was introduced in January 2015 with no cosponsors and died in a House subcommittee without a hearing, vote, or floor action.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have ordered the Justice Department to collect records of every federal and state civil, administrative, and criminal action against corporations and their officials where fines of $1,000 or more were possible, and post them on a public website covering all corporations with over $1 billion in annual revenue. It also required an annual report to Congress counting enforcement actions and their outcomes. The goal was to let consumers, workers, investors, and communities see a company's record of lawbreaking before they buy, invest, or take a job. The bill never advanced past its initial committee referral.
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary people who buy from, work for, invest in, or live near large corporations. A single public database of criminal convictions, civil penalties, and settlements would let consumers check a company's track record, investors price risk, and communities and regulators see patterns of repeat misconduct that are now scattered across agency dockets, press releases, and paywalled court records.

how_it_helps.text: Directs the Attorney General to gather data on all federal and state administrative, civil, and criminal proceedings against corporations or corporate officials involving felony or misdemeanor charges, or civil charges with potential fines of $1,000 or more.

Requires a publicly available website listing improper conduct by every corporation with annual revenues over $1 billion, including the agency bringing the charge, the charge itself, the company and its parent company, and the outcome — convictions, plea agreements, consent decrees, fines, or findings of innocence.

Requires an annual report to Congress detailing the number of civil, administrative, and criminal enforcement actions against corporations and corporate officials, and how each was resolved, including the size and category of penalties.

Requires every federal department and agency to report its enforcement actions to the Justice Department in a uniform format, and lets agency officials enter and update their own records directly in the database.

analysis.who_pays: Large corporations and their officials, whose misconduct records would become instantly searchable by the public. Federal agencies would bear the administrative work of reporting their enforcement actions in a standard format and maintaining their entries.

drawbacks.text: The public database covers only corporations with more than $1 billion in annual revenue, so a company could keep misconduct out of the flagship public site simply by being smaller — and the Justice Department decides the revenue rules.

The database lists charges, not just final judgments, including civil charges with potential fines of $1,000 or more; a company could appear in the public database over an allegation that was later dismissed or resolved in its favor, though the record does include findings of innocence and outcomes.

Federal agencies would face ongoing reporting and data-entry work to feed the database in a uniform format, and the bill explicitly creates no new cause of action, so it changes no penalties — it only publicizes existing enforcement.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit is real but indirect: better information does not itself stop corporate crime, but it lets consumers, investors, journalists, and prosecutors see a company's full record in one place, which raises the reputational price of repeated misconduct. The costs are modest — administrative burden on agencies and some reputational noise for companies accused but not convicted. The bill's narrow public coverage ($1 billion-plus corporations) limits both its reach and its downside. On balance a low-cost transparency measure whose main barrier was never design but scheduling.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Judiciary Committee and its Crime subcommittee on day one, got no cosponsors, no hearing, no markup, and no vote before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. John Conyers Jr. of Michigan introduced the Corporate Crime Database Act on January 6, 2015, the first day of the 114th Congress.
The bill was referred to the House Judiciary Committee and also to the Committee on Oversight and Government Reform, a dual referral that requires two committees to act.
On January 22, 2015, it was referred to the Judiciary Committee's Subcommittee on Crime, Terrorism, Homeland Security, and Investigations — its last recorded action.
The bill attracted no cosponsors, and no further action, hearing, or vote was ever recorded before the 114th Congress ended on January 3, 2017.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Large corporations with revenues over $1 billion are better off, since no public, searchable record of their criminal and civil enforcement history was created. The bill's sponsor spent the session with a bill that never moved; consumers and investors gained nothing.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Large corporations whose records stay scattered

for.name: Rep. John Conyers Jr.
for.what_they_did: Introduced the Corporate Crime Database Act and delivered introductory remarks on it the day it was filed.

against.name: House Judiciary Committee leadership
against.what_they_did: Referred the bill to its Crime subcommittee on January 22, 2015, and scheduled no hearing, markup, or vote on it for the rest of the two-year Congress.

against.name: House Oversight and Government Reform Committee leadership
against.what_they_did: Received the bill by dual referral in January 2015 and took no recorded action on it during the Congress.

sides.party_line_note: No vote was ever recorded and no opposition is documented; the bill's only barrier visible in the record was inaction — it drew zero cosponsors from either party and never left committee.

industries.industry: Large corporations (over $1 billion in annual revenue)
industries.note: The bill would have put every felony, misdemeanor, and significant civil charge against them and their officials on one public, searchable site, including parent-company links that make it harder to bury misconduct in a subsidiary. The reputational exposure was the bill's entire cost to them — it creates no new penalties.

industries.industry: Small and mid-sized companies (under $1 billion revenue)
industries.note: They would be excluded from the public website covering $1 billion-plus corporations, though the underlying data collection covers proceedings against any corporation, leaving a data asymmetry in which the biggest firms face the most public scrutiny.
